chapter_theme: The book's second twenty verses keep its form of three sweet things, often ranked from 'foremost sweet' to 'nothing sweeter', and spread it over giver and asker, king and servant, householder and renouncer, so that restraint of speech and desire, honour, and faithfulness to what others entrust are presented as pleasures rather than duties.

21.reading: The verse names three things sweet: living without seizing wealth held in another's hand, doing dharma and putting away what is not dharma, and living with the discernment never to join unworthy, deluded men, even by forgetting.
21.nuance: The third item asks for more than avoidance: மறந்தேயும் ('even by forgetting') makes keeping out of bad company a matter of trained discernment (திறம்), not of a single decision.

items.claim: living without seizing wealth that is in another's hand is sweet
doing dharma and putting away what is not dharma is sweet

items.thing: மறந்தேயும் மாணா மயரிகள் சேராத் திறந்தெரிந்து வாழ்தல்
items.claim: living with the discernment never to join unworthy, deluded men, even through forgetfulness, is sweet

22.reading: The verse names three things sweet: giving with knowledge of one's income, a zeal that does not make one another's dependant, and living without swerving as one who does not do what he craves even when it would delight him greatly.
22.nuance: Line 2 reads பங்கு ('share') where tamilvu reads பாங்கு ('side'); on either reading the zeal is one that does not hang on someone else. All three items keep a person inside his own measure: of income, of independence, of desire.

items.claim: giving while knowing one's income is sweet
a zeal that does not become someone else's portion or dependant is sweet

items.thing: பெருவகைத் தாயினும் பெட்டவை செய்யார் திரிபின்றி வாழ்தல்
items.claim: living without deviating, not doing what one craves even when it would give great delight, is sweet

23.reading: The verse names as very sweet digging a charity tank together with a grove, as foremost sweet giving gold together with cows to brahmins, and as sweet leaving the சூதர் who, not fearing even sin, speak the language of a grasping trade.
23.nuance: சூதர் may be gamblers (சூது) or men who deceive with speech; பற்றுந் தொழில்மொழி ('speech of a grasping trade') fits either, and the line does not settle which. The verse grades its items (மிக, முன்), and the gift to brahmins is the one called foremost.

items.claim: digging a public charity tank along with a grove is very sweet
giving gold together with cows to brahmins is foremost sweet

items.thing: பாவமும் அஞ்சாராய்ப் பற்றுந் தொழில்மொழிச் சூதரைச் சோர்தல்
items.claim: leaving the சூதர், who do not fear sin and whose talk serves a grasping trade, is sweet

norm.note: a gift norm of the period that names brahmins as the foremost recipients of cows and gold

24.reading: The verse names three things sweet: the austerity of one who wants to win and yet does not rage, the forbearance of one who carries a thing through as far as his strength allows, and doing what is to be done without craving what one lacks and grieving in distress.
24.nuance: Calling the first item நோன்பு, a word for austerity, makes holding back anger in a contest a kind of penance. ஒன்று உய்ப்பான் in line 2 is compressed; 'one who sees a single thing through' is a reading, not a certainty.

items.claim: the austerity of one who, though he wants to win, does not rage is sweet
the forbearance of one who carries a thing through as far as he is able is sweet

items.thing: இல்லாது காமுற் றிரங்கி இடர்ப்படார் செய்வது செய்தல்
items.claim: doing what is to be done, without longing for what one lacks and suffering in grief, is sweet

25.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet curbing the craving of the five senses, as sweet keeping away from the unlearned even when wealth would come to hand, and as sweet leaving without embracing men of unsteady views and no self-containment.
25.nuance: The first item turns inward and the other two outward: the senses are a gate to be guarded and so is one's company, and the second item sets a price on the guarding, wealth given up.

items.claim: curbing the craving that comes through the five senses is foremost sweet
keeping away from the unlearned, even if wealth would come into one's hand, is sweet

items.thing: நில்லாத காட்சி நிறையில் மனிதரைப் புல்லா விடுதல்
items.claim: leaving, without embracing, men whose views do not hold and who have no self-containment is sweet

26.reading: The verse names as sweet the worth of not killing the hope of those who come to one in desire, as very sweet the spirit that will not live where it is held in no regard, and as sweetest of all a bond that in no way hides what it can give.
26.nuance: The first and last items are about the giver and frame the middle one about honour, so the giver's open hand and the self-respect that will not cringe are made one temper. கரவாத names the Kural's fault of concealment (கரவு) by its absence.

items.claim: not killing the hope of those who came to one in desire is sweet
the spirit that will not live where it is not held in regard is very sweet
nothing is sweeter than a bond that does not hide, in any way, what it is able to give

27.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet the noble bearing of one who gives gifts and not living on when dishonour comes, and as sweet taking what has lasting worth by the proper manner of receiving, as those do who do not make much of what is lacking.
27.nuance: ஊனங் கொண்டாடார் is hard: 'those who do not celebrate a defect' is the plainest sense, but the line could also mean those who do not dwell on their losses. கோள்முறையாற் கோடல் uses the grammarians' word for a pupil's receiving of instruction (கோடல்), so the third item may be about receiving teaching; this is a reading, not a certainty.

items.claim: the noble bearing of one who gives gifts is foremost sweet
not living on when dishonour comes is foremost sweet

items.thing: ஊனங்கொண் டாடார் உறுதி உடையவை கோள்முறையாற் கோடல்
items.claim: taking what has lasting worth by the right manner of receiving, without making much of defects, is sweet

28.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not going about crying to others to relieve one's distress, as sweet living mindful that Death's coming is real, and as sweetest of all the judgment of one who speaks no wrong even when his fortune is falling.
28.nuance: All three items face loss: distress one could beg relief from, death, and ruin of fortune. The closing item makes integrity of speech under ruin the sweetest.

items.claim: not going about asking others to relieve one's distress is foremost sweet
living with the thought that Death's coming is real is sweet
nothing is sweeter than the discernment that speaks no wrong even when one's fortune is being destroyed

29.reading: The verse names three things sweet: living with the base put out of one's hands, zeal born of thinking of rising high, and living in brightness without speaking in scorn of people as lowly.
29.nuance: The aspiration in the middle is fenced on both sides: one leaves the base but does not scorn the lowly. Line 1 is nearly the opening line of Thirikadugam 77.

items.claim: living with the base let go of is sweet
zeal arising from thinking of rising high is sweet

items.thing: எளியர் இவரென் றிகழ்ந்துரையா ராகி ஒளிபட வாழ்தல்
items.claim: living in brightness, without speaking scornfully of anyone as lowly, is sweet

30.reading: The verse names as very sweet living with the worth of a kindness weighed, as sweet the excellence of saying nothing crooked in the assembly, and as finest of all the goodness that does not seize a thing given in trust on the thought 'who knew of it then?'
30.nuance: நன்றிப் பயன்தூக்கி most likely means weighing a kindness received, as gratitude does; it could be read as weighing the return before doing good, but the verse's other items, both about honesty owed to others, favour gratitude. The third item names the temptation precisely: the deposit has no witness left.

items.claim: living with the worth of a kindness weighed is very sweet
the excellence of speaking nothing crooked in the assembly is sweet
nothing is finer than the goodness that does not seize a deposit, thinking no one knew of it at the time

31.reading: The verse names three things sweet: the strength that does not let the sorrow of those who came for refuge grow, doing what one must do even by borrowing, and, however excellent one's learning by listening, speaking only after examining and knowing.
31.nuance: செய்வன ('what is to be done') is not specified; with the first item about refugees it most naturally covers duties of help, so the second item would accept debt as the price of duty. The third denies that learning excuses one from examining.

items.claim: the strength that does not let the sorrow of those who came for refuge grow is sweet
doing what is to be done even by taking a loan is sweet
speaking after examining and knowing, even for those whose learning by listening is excellent, is very sweet

32.reading: The verse names as sweet the counsel on a task given by those who know all its surroundings, as foremost sweet not living under a king who has no care, and as finest of all the loyalty that does not plot harm against those who trusted one.
32.nuance: பற்றமையா வேந்தன் may be a king who has no regard for his people or for his servants; either way the servant is free, even advised, to leave. Line 3 (தெற்றென இன்றித் தெளிந்தாரை) is compressed: 'those who trusted without asking for certainty' is a reading.

items.claim: the substance of a task as told by those who know everything around it is sweet
not living under a king who lacks care is foremost sweet
nothing is finer than a loyalty that does not urge harm on those who trusted one

33.reading: The verse names as very sweet the zeal of conducting oneself in ways the town does not resent, as foremost sweet the effort that never sits idle by itself, and as sweet checking the army of great kings who do not give way in the crowded battle.
33.nuance: The list moves from the town to the self to the battlefield, so the same exertion is praised as civic conduct, as industry and as a warrior's stand.

items.claim: the zeal of acting in ways the town does not resent is very sweet
the effort that does not sit idle of its own accord is foremost sweet

items.thing: வாய்மயங்கு மண்டமருள் மாறாத மாமன்னர் தானை தடுத்தல்
items.claim: checking, in the thick of battle, the army of great kings who do not turn back is sweet

34.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not going about at night, as sweet speaking without a slip whenever one speaks, and as sweet leaving, not taking up, the friendship of worthless people even when they embrace one.
34.nuance: வழங்காமை could also mean not giving at night, but with எல்லிப் பொழுது 'not moving about after dark' is the likelier sense. The third item names the hard case: the worthless friend who is affectionate.

items.claim: not going about at night is foremost sweet
speaking without a slip when one speaks is sweet

items.thing: புல்லிக் கொளினும் பொருளல்லார் தங்கேண்மை கொள்ளர் விடுதல்
items.claim: leaving, without taking, the friendship of worthless people even if they embrace one is sweet

35.reading: For kings with victorious spears the verse names as sweet learning the facts by spying through a spy, doing justice after examining everything fully, and knowing how to share out, with attachment, to all living beings.
35.nuance: This is the one verse of the chapter that names its audience (வேந்தர்க்கு). Line 3 is obscure: பற்றினலாய் and பாத்தூற்று are not clear, and 'sharing out to all beings' rests on பாத்து ('dividing'); line 4 (வெற்வேறில்) is corrupt.

items.claim: for a king, learning the facts by spying through a spy is foremost sweet
for a king, doing justice after examining everything fully is foremost sweet
for a king, knowing the way of sharing out to all living beings is sweet

36.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet not speaking out of twisted envy, as sweet living upright after crushing and driving out anger, and as sweet letting go, without snatching, of whatever one sees and desires.
36.nuance: The first item faults envy voiced (உரையாமை), not envy felt; the list runs from tongue to temper to hand.

items.claim: not speaking out of twisted envy is foremost sweet
living upright, having crushed and driven out anger, is sweet

items.thing: கவ்வித்தாங் கொண்டுதாங் கண்டது காமுற்று வவ்வார் விடுதல்
items.claim: letting go, not snatching and grabbing, what one sees and desires is sweet

37.reading: The verse names as sweet knowing youth to be old age, hearing that one's kin are free of fear, and knowing as poison women with broad, soft, bamboo-like shoulders and the grace of tender shoots.
37.domain_note: a man who would master desire
37.nuance: The first and third items are renunciant insights that see through youth and through desire; the second, about kin, belongs to the householder and sits oddly between them. The third speaks of women only as objects of a man's desire.

items.claim: knowing youth to be old age is sweet
hearing that one's kin are free of fear is sweet

items.thing: தடமென் பணைத்தோள் தளிரிய லாரை விடமென் றுணர்தல்
items.claim: the verse names as sweet a man's knowing as poison women with broad soft shoulders and tender grace

norm.note: a renunciant view of the period that names women's bodies as poison to the man who desires them

38.reading: The verse names as sweet the excellence of weapons for one who has few men and as foremost sweet the warlike daring of one who has friends, and reports that the feast for guests of one whose kin stand by him is held sweet beyond all measure.
38.nuance: Each item is conditional on what one has: few men, then weapons; friends, then enmity can be taken on; kin, then the feast. The last item is reported with என்ப ('they say') and given the strongest praise, so the household's hospitality is ranked above the fighter's strengths.

items.claim: for one with few men, the excellence of weapons is sweet
for one who has friends, the daring to take on enemies is foremost sweet
the feast for guests of one whose kin are on his side is said to be sweet in every measure

39.reading: The verse names as foremost sweet that one who eats by going for alms does not clamour, as sweet the dignity of not grieving while living in a borrowed lodging, and as sweet having no want that, from great greed, abandons dharma.
39.nuance: துச்சில் is the Kural's word (340) for the body as the soul's borrowed lodging; the second item can be read literally, of a poor man in borrowed rooms, or with that image. The third item says poverty (ஒற்கம்) is not itself the fault; the fault is the want that greed turns into abandoning dharma.

items.claim: that one who lives by going for alms does not clamour is foremost sweet
the dignity of not sinking into grief while living in a borrowed lodging is sweet

items.thing: உற்றபே ராசை கருதி அறனொரூஉம் ஒற்கம் இலாமை
items.claim: being free of the want that, driven by great greed, abandons dharma is sweet

40.reading: The verse names as sweet living on in one's own town even at a tenfold cost, as very sweet the excellence of not pounding and eating the seed-grain, and as sweetest of all the firm core of learning, faultlessly and over many days, what has worth.
40.nuance: பத்துக் கொடுத்தும் is unclear: 'even paying tenfold' or 'even giving up a tenth'. The first two items are about holding on in hard times, to one's place and to next year's seed, and the book's last item adds learning as the third thing one does not consume.

items.claim: living on in one's own town even at the cost of paying ten is sweet
the excellence of not pounding and eating the seed-grain is very sweet

items.thing: பற்பல நாளும் பழுதின்றிப் பாங்குடைய கற்றலிற் காழ
items.claim: nothing is sweeter than the firm core of learning what has worth, faultlessly, over many days

links.note: Iniyavai calls giving with knowledge of one's income sweet; Innaa 39 counts the liberality of one with nothing to give as painful. They say the same thing from two sides.
links.teaches: Read as a pair, the twin books fix one measure for giving from opposite ends: the pleasure lies inside one's income and the pain begins outside it.

links.note: Naladiyar 65 calls the gift of one without wealth the true fruit of giving; Iniyavai calls giving within one's income sweet.
links.teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on where giving is best: the quatrain prizes the gift that strains one's means, while this verse prizes the gift that stays within them.
links.list_adds: It sets measured giving beside independence from others and refusal of indulgence, so giving is ranked as one form of self-limitation rather than a test of sacrifice.

links.note: Iniyavai calls giving cows and gold to brahmins foremost sweet; Innaa 21 counts the speech of a brahmin without Vedic recitation as painful, and giving to the never-content as painful.
links.teaches: Together the twin books make the brahmin a privileged recipient but not an unconditional one: the Innaa line ties his standing to recitation, a condition this verse leaves out.

links.note: Naladiyar 65 calls true patience that of a strong man able to punish; Iniyavai calls sweet the austerity of one who wants to win and does not rage.
links.teaches: Both place the worth of restraint where the urge to strike is live, and the pair shows the group treating anger held back in a contest as a form of penance.
links.list_adds: It names the restraint நோன்பு, a word of austerity, and sets it beside endurance and freedom from craving, so mastering anger is filed with ascetic practice.

links.note: Kural 343, in the chapter on renunciation, says the field of the five senses must be crushed and all desires let go at once; Iniyavai calls curbing the craving of the five senses foremost sweet, with no renouncer named.
links.teaches: The pair shows sense-restraint moving from the renouncer's whole programme in the Kural to a first pleasure open to anyone, its demand softened from abandoning to curbing.
links.list_adds: It ranks sense-restraint first and pairs it with keeping away from the unlearned and the unsteady, so the inner gate and the outer company are guarded together.

links.note: Naladiyar 111 says refusing what one cannot give is no fault, but letting an asker's hope (நசை) die after keeping him waiting is worse than ingratitude; Iniyavai calls not killing the hope (நசை) of those who come sweet.
links.teaches: Both judge a giver by what happens to the asker's hope, the quatrain condemning its slow killing by false promise and the verse praising its keeping, so honesty to the hope matters as much as the gift.
links.list_adds: It ties keeping askers' hope to a spirit that will not live without regard and a bond that hides nothing, so generosity is grouped with self-respect rather than with promise-keeping.

links.note: Kural 966 asks why one should stand behind those who scorn one; Iniyavai calls very sweet the spirit that will not live where it is held in no regard.
links.teaches: The couplet argues from the loss of praise and heaven, while the verse calls the refusal a pleasure in itself, so the pair shows honour defended first by reckoning and then by taste.
links.list_adds: It places the refusal to live without regard between two items on giving, so the self-respect of the giver and of the one who will not cringe are made one temper.

links.note: Kural 969 says those like the yak give up life when honour is lost; Iniyavai calls not living on when dishonour comes foremost sweet.
links.teaches: The verse names as a pleasure what the couplet presents as the nature of a rare kind of person, so the pair shows an admired temperament turned into something anyone may prefer.
links.list_adds: It sets dying rather than living dishonoured between the giver's bearing and right receiving, so honour is framed by how one gives and how one takes.

links.note: Kural 1066 says even asking water for a cow is the most degrading thing for the tongue; Iniyavai calls not going about asking others to relieve one's distress foremost sweet.
links.teaches: The pair values not asking from both sides, as disgrace avoided and as the first of pleasures, and the verse's ஆற்றாமை widens it from asking for goods to asking for relief.
links.list_adds: It ranks not asking first and follows it with remembering death and holding to right speech under ruin, so refusing to beg sits among the disciplines of a man facing loss.

links.note: Kural 113 says to let go at once of gain that comes from leaving fairness; Iniyavai calls sweetest the discernment that speaks no wrong even when one's fortune is being destroyed.
links.teaches: The couplet refuses unfair gain and the verse refuses unfair speech even to escape ruin, so the pair carries fairness from getting to speaking under loss.
links.list_adds: It puts this item last as the sweetest of three, after not begging and remembering death, so integrity under ruin outranks the other two.

links.note: Kural 596 says whatever one thinks, think of rising; Iniyavai calls sweet the zeal born of thinking of rising, using the couplet's own word உயர்வுள்ளி.
links.teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's phrase and names what the thought produces, zeal, so the pair shows aspiration as the root and ஊக்கம் as its fruit.
links.list_adds: It brackets the thought of rising between leaving the base and not scorning the lowly, so aspiration is hedged on both sides by conduct toward others.

links.note: Thirikadugam 77 opens with கயவரைக் கையிகந்து வாழ்தல் and makes it a mark of those whose family has no stain; Iniyavai 29 opens with கயவரைக் கைகழிந்து வாழ்தல் and calls it sweet.
links.teaches: The near-identical line shows a saying circulating between the counted works, and the different predicates show each bending it: a sign of good birth in one, a pleasure open to anyone in the other.

links.note: Innaa 40 counts seizing a deposit (அடைக்கலம் வவ்வுதல்) as painful; Iniyavai calls the goodness that does not seize a deposit the finest. They say the same thing from two sides.
links.teaches: The Iniyavai line adds the temptation the Innaa line omits, the thought that no one knew of it, so the pair shows the deposit as a test of honesty without witnesses.

links.note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit of a kindness count a millet's worth as a palm; Iniyavai calls living with the fruit of a kindness weighed very sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet says how to weigh a kindness and the verse says living by that weighing is a pleasure, so the pair shows gratitude as a habit of measuring that becomes a way of life.
links.list_adds: It joins gratitude to honest speech in the assembly and keeping a deposit, so the three become one virtue of rendering to each what is owed.

links.note: Kural 417 says those whose listening is gathered on close study do not speak folly even when they misunderstand; Iniyavai says even those of excellent learning by listening should speak only after examining.
links.teaches: The couplet trusts deep listening to protect speech even through error, while the verse still asks the learned to examine first, so the pair shows the counted work refusing learning as a guarantee.
links.list_adds: It ranks examined speech with protecting refugees and doing one's duties even on borrowed money, so careful speech is made a duty owed to others.

links.note: Kural 220 says loss through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Iniyavai calls doing what is to be done even by borrowing sweet, if செய்வன covers duties of help.
links.teaches: The couplet's extreme, selling oneself, appears here in a household form, taking a loan, so the pair shows the ethics group pricing duty to others in debt.
links.list_adds: It sets duties done on credit beside protecting those who came for refuge, so borrowing to do one's part is grouped with protection rather than prudence.

links.note: Purananuru 330 praises one man who, sword raised, stopped a king's army from passing him as the shore stops the sea; Iniyavai calls checking the army of great kings in the crowded battle sweet.
links.teaches: The Purananuru makes the stand one hero's glory, and the counted verse files it with civic zeal and tireless effort, showing heroic memory folded into a general ethic of exertion.

links.note: Kural 800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at the cost of a gift; Iniyavai calls sweet leaving the friendship of the worthless even when they embrace one.
links.teaches: The couplet counts the cost of leaving in goods and the verse in affection refused, so the pair shows two prices a man may pay to be free of an unworthy friend.
links.list_adds: It closes a list that begins with keeping off the roads at night and speaking without slips, so ending a bad friendship is grouped with other kinds of self-guarding.

links.note: Kural 588 says to confirm what one spy reports through another (ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி); Iniyavai calls sweet for kings learning facts ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி.
links.teaches: The verse's compressed phrase echoes the couplet's, and read through it the item can mean checking one spy by another, not merely using one.
links.list_adds: It sets spying beside full inquiry before judgment and sharing with all beings, so intelligence is ranked with justice and care as one royal pleasure.

links.note: Kural 167 says the goddess shows the man of twisted envy (அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு) to her elder sister; Iniyavai calls not speaking out of twisted envy foremost sweet, in the same words.
links.teaches: The couplet punishes envy held and the verse praises envy unspoken, so the pair shows the ethics group separating the feeling from its voicing and treating restraint of the tongue as a partial cure.
links.list_adds: It puts restraint of envious speech first, ahead of conquered anger and refusing to snatch, ranking a fault of the tongue above faults of temper and hand.

links.note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; Iniyavai calls knowing youth to be old age sweet.
links.teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, early renunciation, that the verse leaves implicit, and the verse calls that foresight sweet rather than grim.
links.list_adds: It joins the foresight of age to seeing desire as poison and to the comfort of safe kin, so two renunciant insights are framed by a household one.

links.note: Kural 524 says the fruit of wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin; Iniyavai says the feast for guests of one whose kin stand by him is sweet beyond measure.
links.teaches: The couplet makes kin the use of wealth and the verse names the guest-feast as the moment that use shows, so the pair links kinship to hospitality.
links.list_adds: It ranks the kin-supported feast above the fighter's weapons and allies with எத்துணையும் ஆற்ற, so the house's hospitality outranks martial strength.

links.note: Kural 1060 says the one who asks must not be angry; Iniyavai calls it foremost sweet that one who lives by alms does not clamour.
links.teaches: Both place restraint on the receiver rather than the giver, and the pair shows the ethics group laying a duty on the needy as well as on the rich.
links.list_adds: It moves the rule from askers in general to the one who lives by alms and joins it to calm in a borrowed lodging, so it becomes part of a renouncer's poverty.

links.note: Kural 340 calls the soul a lodger in a borrowed corner (துச்சில்) of the body; Iniyavai calls sweet not grieving while living in a துச்சில்.
links.teaches: Read through the couplet, the verse's lodger may be the soul in the body as well as a poor man in borrowed rooms, which would make its item an image of calm about mortality.
links.list_adds: It sets the lodger's calm between the alms-eater's restraint and freedom from greedy want, so the image is read inside a renouncer's poverty.

links.note: Kural 391 says to learn faultlessly what should be learned and stand by it; Iniyavai calls the firm core of learning what has worth, faultlessly and over many days, the sweetest thing.
links.teaches: The verse adds duration and names the result காழ், a hard core, so the pair shows flawless learning as something that hardens over time.
links.list_adds: It closes the book on learning after staying in one's town at a cost and not eating the seed-grain, so learning is grouped with the household's ways of keeping what feeds the future.

source_issues: 22 line 2: பங்கு where tamilvu reads பாங்கு; the sense changes little.
28 line 2: வாழ்வனிதே looks like a misprint for வாழ்வினிதே.
34 line 4: கொள்ளர் is most likely கொள்ளார்.
35 line 3: பற்றினலாய் and பாத்தூற்று are obscure, possibly corrupt; line 4 வெற்வேறில் is corrupt (Project Madurai prints the variant வெற்றல் வேல்).
38 line 4: சுற்றா is an irregular form, read as சுற்றம்.
40 line 2: வித்துற்குற் றுண்ணா is irregularly written; read as வித்து குற்று உண்ணா, not pounding and eating the seed-grain.
